otto-idea-of-holy-1923:
Rudolf Otto was a German theologian whose Idea of the Holy, in this 1923 English edition, changed the study of religion worldwide. Otto argues that religion rests on an experience that reason alone cannot capture. He names that core the numinous, from the Latin word for divine power.

The numinous, he says, is a mystery at once fearful and fascinating, the mysterium tremendum that makes worshippers tremble and draw near. He finds it in Hebrew prophets, Hindu hymns, and the silence of Quaker worship alike. His book founded the modern phenomenology of religion, the study of faith as it is felt.
goldsack-selections-muhammadan-tradition:
William Goldsack was a missionary scholar in Bengal who translated Islamic texts for Christian and general readers. His Selections from Muhammadan Traditions, published in 1923, offers classified English selections from the six canonical hadith collections. Hadith are the recorded sayings and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad.

Goldsack arranges traditions from Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, and others by subject, from prayer to trade to family life. A reader can see what the tradition teaches on a topic without searching the vast Arabic collections. The book served missionaries and students as a handy, ordered gateway to Islam's second source.
machen-christianity-and-liberalism-1923:
Machen's Christianity and Liberalism, published in 1923, is the fundamentalist manifesto of the American church fights of the 1920s. Its claim is blunt: liberalism is not a kind of Christianity but a different religion entirely. Machen wrote it while Princeton Seminary slid toward the split he would soon lead.

He compares the two faiths on God, man, the Bible, Christ, salvation, and the church, finding them opposed at every point. Liberalism, he says, rests on naturalism, the denial that God acts in history in supernatural ways. The book still anchors conservative arguments about the boundaries of the faith.
carpzov-practica-nova-1723:
Benedict Carpzov was a Saxon judge whose Practica Nova, in this 1723 edition, codified criminal practice for the German courts. The work covers crimes and their proofs in the Roman and Saxon legal tradition. Under its rules, Saxon witch trials were conducted for generations.

Carpzov treats witchcraft as a crime of the gravest kind, to be proved by confession, witnesses, and strict legal form. His fame rested on the sheer number of cases his court decided under his guidance. Legal historians call him the most-cited criminalist of the witch-hunt era, a name that stands for its system at full strength.
torreblanca-daemonologia-1623:
Francisco Torreblanca Villalpando was a Spanish jurist whose Daemonologia appeared in 1623. Its full Latin title promises a treatise on magic natural, demonic, licit, and illicit, sorted into kinds. Torreblanca wrote for a Spain where the Inquisition watched occult practice closely.

He divides wonders into those God allows, those nature hides, and those demons fake, and assigns each its lawful response. His care in sorting licit natural magic from forbidden demonic arts shows the period's legal mind at its sharpest. The book is a prime source for Spanish demonology in the age of the great trials.
robson-fixed-stars-and-constellations-19:
Vivian Robson was a British astrologer and librarian whose Fixed Stars and Constellations in Astrology appeared in 1923. The book gathers the lore of the fixed stars, the bright stars beyond the planets, into one compendium. It became the standard modern reference for stellar astrology.

Robson lists each star's position, nature, and reputed effects on health, fortune, and character, drawn from Ptolemy and the long tradition after him. He sorts a scattered inheritance of Greek, Arab, and modern claims into usable order. Astrologers still reach for Robson first when a chart raises a question about the fixed stars.
osty-supernormal-faculties-in-man-1923:
Eugène Osty, a French doctor who led a Paris institute for psychical study, published Supernormal Faculties in Man in 1923. Osty reported tests with people said to know facts they could not have learned in normal ways. He used the term supernormal for powers beyond the usual senses.

Case studies follow subjects through sittings where they described hidden objects, past events, and distant scenes. Osty tried to rule out fraud and lucky guessing, and he set out rules for such tests. His work reflects the French branch of psychical research, which leaned toward careful case work in the lab and the study room.
proudhon-general-idea-revolution-robinso:
John Beverley Robinson published his translation of Proudhon's General Idea of the Revolution in the Nineteenth Century in 1923. Proudhon wrote the work in 1851, from a French prison cell, as Louis Napoleon tightened his grip. It is his fullest plan for a free society.

Proudhon proposed ending rule by the state and letting work and trade run by free pact. He called for free credit, shared banks, and loose unions of towns and workshops. Robinson, an American writer, kept the case clear in English. The book links Proudhon's early attack on property to the shared, local plans that later rebels took up across Europe.
goldman-my-disillusionment-russia-1923:
Emma Goldman published My Disillusionment in Russia in 1923. Goldman had sailed to Soviet Russia in 1919, deported from the United States as a dangerous radical. She went as a friend of the revolution and left, two years later, as its critic.

Goldman described the crushing of free unions, the jailing of anarchists, and the Kronstadt sailors' revolt and its bloody end. She told how Bolshevik power, in her account, replaced one tyranny with another. The book was among the first breaks with Bolshevism from within the revolutionary left. Her firsthand scenes and names gave the account weight that later histories have confirmed in large part.
lawrence-birds-beasts-flowers-1923:
D. H. Lawrence wrote most of Birds, Beasts and Flowers during his travels in Italy, New Mexico, and Australia. The collection appeared in 1923, after he had left England for good. Lawrence arranged the poems by their subjects, as the title announces.

The poems watch plants and animals with fierce attention. A snake drinking at a trough in Sicily shames the poet's fearful education. Figs, bats, kangaroos, and dark Bavarian gentians all appear, each treated as a living otherness to respect. Lawrence rejected smooth traditional forms for free, breathing rhythms. Many readers call this his finest book of poems.
shaw-saint-joan-1923:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Saint Joan in 1923, soon after the Catholic Church made Joan of Arc a saint. Shaw, then in his sixties, treated Joan not as a plaster saint but as a practical, stubborn genius. He called the play a chronicle play in six scenes and an epilogue.

The action follows Joan from Domrémy, where her voices send her to the French court, through her victories and capture. Church and state join to try her for heresy, and she is burned at the stake. An epilogue set years later shows her judges regretting their work. Shaw argues that institutions destroy the very saints they later honor.
webster-duchess-malfi-1623:
John Webster wrote The Duchess of Malfi around 1613, drawing on an Italian tale of a widowed duchess murdered by her brothers. The play was performed by the King's Men and printed in 1623. Webster, a London coachmaker's son, wrote only a handful of plays, but two of them are masterpieces.

The Duchess secretly marries her steward, Antonio, and bears his children while hiding the marriage for years. Her brothers, a cardinal and the twisted Ferdinand, hire the malcontent Bosola to spy on her. Discovery leads to imprisonment, madness, and murder staged with grim theatrical invention. The play mixes horror with real pity, and many call it the crown of Jacobean tragedy.
cummings-tulips-and-chimneys-1923:
The first book of poems by E. E. Cummings was Tulips and Chimneys, published in 1923. Cummings had served as an ambulance driver in the First World War and been held in a French detention camp. His Harvard education and war experience both feed the poems.

The collection mixes sonnets, songs, and portraits with early experiments in spacing and broken lines. Cummings mocks stuffed shirts and celebrates spring, lovers, and street life in the same breath. Readers met a voice already reshaping the lyric from inside: playful, tender, and formally daring. The publisher cut some poems, but the book still marks the beginning of Cummings's lifelong reinvention of poetry.
millay-harp-weaver-1923:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published The Harp-Weaver and Other Poems in 1923, and it won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry. Millay was the first woman to win that prize. The book catches her in her prime, when her sonnets were being memorized across America.

The title ballad tells of a poor mother who weaves fine clothes for her son on a magic harp as she dies. Behind its fairy-tale shape sits real poverty Millay knew from her own childhood. The volume also holds a celebrated sonnet sequence on love and loss. Ballads, lyrics, and sonnets together make this the fullest single display of Millay's gifts.
hemingway-three-stories-1923:
Ernest Hemingway was a twenty-four-year-old newspaper correspondent in Paris when Three Stories and Ten Poems appeared in 1923. A tiny press printed only three hundred copies. It was his first book, and almost everything he later became is visible in it.

The lead story, Up in Michigan, tells of a young woman's rough sexual awakening in a lumber town. Two more stories introduce Nick Adams, the hero of his later fiction, fishing and soldiering. The ten poems, snapshots of bullfights, executions, and war, are frankly apprentice work. The plain style that would change American prose is already forming. This slim Paris debut is where Hemingway began.
cooper-pioneers-1823:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Pioneers in 1823, the first of the Leatherstocking Tales. Cooper drew on his own family's founding of Cooperstown, New York, and set the story there in 1793, as settlement tamed the wilderness. The novel asks what progress costs, and who pays.

Judge Marmaduke Temple rules the new town, while old Natty Bumppo, the hunter Leatherstocking, watches the forest fall. Settlers slaughter pigeons and net fish wastefully, and Natty is arrested for killing a deer out of season. A young stranger with a hidden claim to the land complicates every plot. Cooper founded the American frontier myth here, with sympathy on both sides of the axe.
frost-new-hampshire-1923:
Robert Frost published New Hampshire in 1923, and it won the first Pulitzer Prize ever given for poetry. The long title poem is a loose, talkative tour of his adopted state. Frost had settled in New Hampshire and Vermont after his years in England, and the state became his poetic ground.

Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, the book's most famous short poem, watches a man pause between a frozen lake and his promises. Fire and Ice weighs how the world might end in nine lines. Two Witches of Cousin County, Paul Bunyan tales in verse, and sharp lyrics fill out the volume. New Hampshire confirmed Frost as America's best-loved living poet, a reputation he kept for forty years.
anderson-many-marriages-1923:
Sherwood Anderson published Many Marriages in 1923, the most outspoken of his novels. Anderson had been through divorces of his own and wrote obsessively about the gap between respectable marriage and inner desire. The book shocked some readers and was banned in places for its frankness.

John Webster, a washing-machine manufacturer in a Wisconsin town, walks through his house at midnight and confesses everything to his daughter. He tells her of his dead wife, his erotic discontent, and his plan to begin life again with his secretary. The confession takes the whole novel, part sermon and part breakdown. Anderson's plain, groping style tries to say what his characters cannot. Many Marriages remains his most daring treatment of marriage.
cather-lost-lady-1923:
A Lost Lady, published by Willa Cather in 1923, centers on Marian Forrester of Sweet Water, Nebraska. Marian is the gracious wife of an older railroad builder, Captain Forrester. A young neighbor, Niel Herbert, watches her life over many years and tells her story.

In Niel's youth Marian seems to embody grace, charm, and the pioneer age at its best. After her husband's ruin and death, she changes in ways that shock her young admirer. Cather treats her with sympathy rather than scorn. The short novel mourns a passing frontier world while showing the strength a woman needed to survive it.
julian-works-wright-vol3-1923:
Wilmer Cave Wright's third Loeb volume of Julian's works came out in 1923, ten years after the first two. It holds the emperor's letters and the fragments of works that survive only in pieces. Julian wrote these texts in the brief reign when he tried to turn the empire back to its old gods.

The chief piece is Against the Galilaeans, his case against the Christians, kept in quotes by Cyril, the church writer who answered it. Julian mocks the claims of the Bible and defends Greek religion and learning. The letters beside it show his rule in daily detail. The volume completes Wright's English Julian.
llull-lover-beloved-peers-1923:
Ramon Llull was the Catalan mystic of the 1200s. His Book of the Lover and the Beloved is a string of 366 short prose poems, one for each day of the year. E. Allison Peers translated the work into English in 1923, with an essay on the life of Llull and his famous Art. The poems stand inside his great romance Blanquerna.

The Lover seeks the Beloved, who is God, through forests of signs, questions, and joy. Each piece is a spark: a dialogue, a sigh, a small parable of longing and praise. Llull drew on the Sufi poets he had read in Mallorca. The book is the sweetest fruit of Catalan mysticism, still read day by day.
fraser-edwards-life-and-teachings-of-tuk:
J. Nelson Fraser and J. F. Edwards wrote The Life and Teaching of Tukaram in 1923, the standard English life of the Marathi poet-saint. The text here is the 1932 reprint of the same work. Tukaram, a grain trader of Dehu in the seventeenth century, sang his faith in thousands of short abhangs to the god Vithoba.

The book tells of his poverty, his lost first wife and child, his visions, and his feud with the Brahmins who threw his poems in the river. It then sets out his teaching through translations of the abhangs: devotion, humility, and the name of God above all rite. Tukaram is Maharashtra's best loved saint. Fraser and Edwards made him known to the English world.
bischoff-die-kabbalah-1923:
Erich Bischoff, a German scholar of the occult and of Jewish learning, wrote Die Kabbalah as a plain introduction to Jewish mysticism and its secret science. The third edition appeared in 1923, with pictures. The book is in German. Bischoff aimed at the general reader who wanted the system whole, without the years of Hebrew it usually demands.

He sets out the ten sefirot, the tree of life, the letters and their numbers, and the schools from the Zohar to the Hasidim. His survey became the standard German popular account of the subject. Plates of seals, trees, and amulets crowd the pages. It shows how the German reading public of the 1920s met the Kabbalah.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-1-182:
Gilbert Burnet, a Scottish bishop who lived at the center of power, wrote the History of His Own Time. The work was published in 1724 to 1734, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1823. The edition runs to six volumes, with passages once suppressed now restored. Burnet's span covers the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution.

Burnet writes as a Whig and a churchman who knew Cromwell's heirs, Charles II, and William III in person. His pages mix high politics with gossip, character, and sharp moral judgment. The result is the great eyewitness history of his age, partisan and priceless at once. Volume one sets that crowded stage.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-2-182:
Volume two continues Gilbert Burnet's History of His Own Time in the Oxford edition of 1823. Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, covers the later Stuart age from a bishop's seat near the throne. The 1823 edition runs to six volumes and restores passages that earlier editors had cut.

Burnet knew the men he judges: kings, ministers, generals, and plotters passed through his life. His narrative of the Restoration and the road to revolution in 1688 is vivid, frank, and openly Whig in sympathy. Scholars quarrel with his bias and quarry his facts in the same breath. Volume two keeps the eyewitness record rolling through a dangerous reign.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-3-182:
Burnet's History of His Own Time reaches volume three in the Oxford edition of 1823, the six-volume set with suppressed passages restored. Gilbert Burnet published the history in 1724 to 1734, drawn from his own diaries and his place at the heart of affairs. He had advised William of Orange and helped prepare the revolution of 1688.

Volume three holds the middle of his long story, from Restoration intrigue toward open crisis. Burnet's pen portraits of the age's leaders are bold, warm, and sometimes unfair, always alive. His history is the great Whig counterpart to Clarendon's royalist epic. Reading both gives the age in stereo. This volume keeps Burnet's side loud and clear.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-4-182:
Volume four of the 1823 Oxford Burnet continues the History of His Own Time, Gilbert Burnet's record of the later Stuart years. The original work appeared in 1724 to 1734, in the years after Burnet's death. The Oxford set fills six volumes and prints passages that the first editors suppressed.

Burnet writes history as a participant with strong loves and hatreds, which is both its spice and its warning. Courts, parliaments, and churches fill his pages, judged by a man who served in all three. The Glorious Revolution, his great cause, draws near as the volumes advance. Volume four carries the crisis forward in the bishop's brisk, knowing voice.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-5-182:
The History of His Own Time moves through volume five in the Oxford edition of 1823. Gilbert Burnet's work, published in 1724 to 1734, narrates England's passage from Restoration to revolution through the eyes of a bishop at the center. The six-volume Oxford edition restores text cut from the first printings.

Volume five stands deep in the reign-shaking events Burnet helped to shape. His account blends state papers, private talk, and his own sermons and counsel to princes. No Whig source of the age is fuller, franker, or more fun to argue with. The narrative here keeps its pace: plots, wars, and successions judged by a man who knew the players by name.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-6-182:
Volume six completes the Oxford edition of 1823 of Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time. Gilbert Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, ends its long arc from the Restoration through the Glorious Revolution. Six volumes, with suppressed passages restored, hold the standard text of the work.

Burnet closes his story as he began it, an insider with opinions he does not hide. William III's wars and settlement fill the later pages, weighed by a bishop who had ridden with the revolution. His history remains the great Whig eyewitness account of the age, set against Clarendon's royalist one. To finish volume six is to close that famous pair of witnesses.
principle-of-relativity-1923:
Methuen issued The Principle of Relativity in 1923, in W. Perrett and G. B. Jeffery's translation. Inside stand the primary papers of relativity by its makers. H. A. Lorentz and Albert Einstein represent the theory's first steps. H. Minkowski contributes Space and Time, his famed address on the new geometry of physics.

H. Weyl's Gravitation and Electricity carries the story into general relativity. Notes by Arnold Sommerfeld help readers through the hard parts. The volume let English readers study the sources, not just summaries. It fixed the canon of early relativity in one binding. Students still use it to meet the founders directly. Few source books match its lineup.
spr-proceedings-vol33-1923:
Parts eighty five through eighty eight form volume thirty three, printed in 1923. The Society for Psychical Research spreads four parts across this single year. Telepathy experiments continue, now a tradition with its own classics. Reports on trance sittings take the largest share, as they long had.

Investigators compare new mediums against the great Piper record. Apparition cases, each with its witnesses and documents, keep their place. The society prints criticism from members who doubt the whole enterprise. Volume thirty three shows the archive in its last full decade. The debate of 1882 to 1930 nears its close here. Its files outlasted every verdict offered on them.
bertrand-traite-somnambulisme-1823:
Alexandre Bertrand wrote his Traite du somnambulisme in French in 1823. Somnambulism, sleepwalking raised by magnetism, is his whole subject. Bertrand sorts its forms and the changes each one brings. His treatise is the first systematic French pathology of magnetic sleep.

A doctor by training, he writes against both blind belief and blind scorn. Cases from the early magnetists receive his cool review. Later French schools of hypnosis built on ground he cleared. The French original stands as the documentary text. Bertrand later turned to other fields, but the treatise kept his name. It shows French medicine weighing the magnetic marvels early. The balance he strikes still reads well.
price-new-geology-1923:
In 1923 George McCready Price published a geology textbook with a startling claim at its center. Price argued that the earth is young and that Noah's Flood, not slow change over ages, shaped the rock layers. He wrote against the view, then held by most geologists, that the same slow forces still at work today explain the past.

Price lays out his case layer by layer, reading fossils and strata as records left by one great flood. Later writers on creation and the Flood built on his scheme, which is why the book is often called the founding text of flood geology. It also shows the sharp clash between faith and science in its day.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol23:
Volume XXIII of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1883, deep into the set's long run. Sermons by leading elders fill the pages, reported word for word as the Journal always promised its readers. The speakers teach a church under legal siege, and quiet resolve rings through the talks.

Yet everyday counsel still shares space with defense of the faith, since the pulpit served both needs each week. The printed volumes let Saints abroad stand, in effect, in the tabernacle with the Utah congregations. Volume XXIII continues the doctrinal record toward its close, three volumes from the end of the whole set.
muir-life-mohammad-weir-1923:
William Muir built The Life of Mohammad from Arabic sources, first in 1861 and revised by T. H. Weir in the 1923 edition. Muir read Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, Waqidi, and Tabari at first hand, a rare feat for a Victorian writer. His critical biography follows the Prophet from Mecca to Medina to the conquest of Arabia.

Muir admired his subject's power while judging the faith by his own Christian lights, and readers have argued with him ever since. The book long served English readers as their fullest life of Mohammad from the sources. It also stands as the public-domain stand-in for the early Sira in English.
rattray-ashanti-1923:
Robert Sutherland Rattray wrote Ashanti in 1923, the foundational ethnography of the Ashanti people of the Gold Coast. Rattray served as the colonial government's own anthropologist in what is now Ghana, recording law and religion at first hand for years. The Golden Stool, soul of the nation, abusua kinship, gods, shrines, and courts fill his account.

Ashanti priests, queen mothers, and elders speak through his pages, explaining custom in their own terms to the reader. Rattray's respect for his sources and his care with their words made the book a model of its kind. A century on, Ashanti remains a first source for the kingdom's religion, law, and social order.
radin-the-winnebago-tribe-1923:
Radin's great monograph on the Winnebago, now called Ho-Chunk, appeared in 1923 in the annual report of the Bureau of American Ethnology. It was the fullest statement of his years of fieldwork with the tribe in Wisconsin and Nebraska.

The study centers on the medicine rite, a major ceremony taught in secret and passed down at great cost. Radin also describes the night-spirits society and prints autobiographies of native thinkers in their own words. His method treated Winnebago men as authors, not just informants. The monograph remains a foundation for the study of Native American religion.
lawrence-ladybird-1923:
The Ladybird, published in 1923, gathers three long stories from Lawrence's post-war years: 'The Ladybird', 'The Fox', and 'The Captain's Doll'. Each turns on power and surrender between men and women in a Europe broken by war.

In the title story, a wounded German count draws an English lady toward a dark, chthonic faith. 'The Fox' sets two women farming alone against a young soldier and the fox that haunts them, toward a shocking end. 'The Captain's Doll' plays the same tensions as comedy. These are among Lawrence's most perfectly made tales, written at the height of his powers.
lawrence-studies-classic-american-1923:
Lawrence's 1923 criticism took on the classic American writers and read them against the grain. His essays on Franklin, Cooper, Poe, Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman became the most famous single book of American literary criticism by an outsider.

Lawrence claims that American literature hides a dark secret: a continent won by violence, and a soul split between innocence and blood. He distrusts what these writers say they mean and hunts what their tales confess. The style is wild, funny, and prophetic. Scholars have argued with his readings ever since, and few have matched their force. The book remade how America read itself.
lawrence-kangaroo-1923:
Lawrence and Frieda spent months in Australia in 1922, and Kangaroo grew directly out of that stay. Published in 1923, it follows Richard Somers, a writer much like Lawrence, settling near Sydney with his wife Harriet.

Somers is courted by 'Kangaroo', a charismatic lawyer building a paramilitary movement of returned soldiers, and by socialists who want him too. He refuses both, and the novel becomes a reckoning with politics, loyalty, and Australia itself. Long passages simply watch the sea and bush with fierce attention. It is the antipodean chapter of Lawrence's search for a new life and a new faith.
conrad-rover-1923:
The Rover, published in 1923, was the last novel Conrad completed, and it has the calm of a farewell. Peyrol, an old buccaneer and brother of the coast, retires to a farm on the French Mediterranean after the Revolution.

England and France are at war, and Peyrol is drawn into one last mission: carrying false dispatches to sea to mislead the British fleet. Around him gather a scarred girl, a patriot, and a naval lieutenant, in a story of sacrifice and quiet honor. Conrad wrote it in his final illness. Its serenity feels earned, like a seaman's last landfall.
anderson-horses-men-1923:
Horses and Men, published in 1923, gathers Anderson's later stories of the American Midwest. Horses run through the book as measures of human worth: creatures of grace beside men cramped by money, shame, or longing.

'The Man Who Became a Woman' tells of a young horse-hand's frightening, tender awakening at a county fair. Other stories follow grooms, trainers, and small-town dreamers in Anderson's halting, musical prose. The racing world gave him some of his finest material. The collection confirms his gift for lives that official America overlooked, told from inside their own confusion and hope.
broad-scientific-thought-1923:
Scientific Thought, published in 1923, is Broad's masterwork on what the new physics means for philosophy at large. Relativity and the quantum age were remaking science's picture of nature, and Broad set out to map the damage and the gains for thought.

He examines space, time, matter, and cause as the new theories rebuilt them, asking which older notions can survive. His manner is slow, exhaustive, and scrupulously fair to every side. Philosophers treated the book as the standard survey of the questions. It shows analytic philosophy learning to take modern physics seriously, concept by concept.
cassirer-substance-function-1923:
Substance and Function, published in English in 1923 with Cassirer's essay on Einstein's relativity, is his critical theory of how science forms its concepts. Ernst Cassirer, the leading neo-Kantian of his generation, argues that modern thought has replaced substance with function.

Older logic built concepts as lists of shared properties, copies of things. Modern mathematics and physics, Cassirer shows, build them as rules and relations: number, function, and field. The appended essay applies the same reading to Einstein, finding relativity a triumph of relational thought. The book is demanding but foundational for the philosophy of science.
veblen-absentee-ownership-1923:
Absentee Ownership, published in 1923, is Thorstein Veblen's last book, subtitled the case of America. The great critic of business returns to his lifelong target: owners who profit without work. He weighs the waste their control imposes on the whole country.

Veblen sets industry, the making of goods, against business, the making of money by managing scarcity and prices. Absentee owners, he argues, hold back production to protect earnings, and America suffers the difference. His prose is sardonic, looping, and remorseless. The book closes his long critique of American business life with undiminished bite. It appeared six years before his death.
parry-second-voyage-northwest-passage-18:
Parry's second Arctic voyage, from 1821 to 1823, sought the passage by Hudson Bay and the straits beyond. His Journal of a Second Voyage appeared in 1824. Two winters in the ice gave the work its special value.

The crews wintered at Winter Island and then at Igloolik, where they lived beside an Inuit community. Parry records Inuit dress, hunting, family life, and language with unusual care. That makes the book a landmark of early Arctic ethnography as well as a voyage narrative. The passage stayed hidden, but the human record of those winters endures. Plates of Inuit dress, tools, and homes give the text lasting worth.
franklin-journey-polar-sea-1823:
John Franklin led an overland expedition from Hudson Bay to the Arctic coast of Canada between 1819 and 1822. His Narrative of a Journey to the Shores of the Polar Sea appeared in 1823. The journey made his name for endurance, at terrible cost.

Franklin's party mapped the Coppermine River and hundreds of miles of coast, then turned back short of food. Starvation, cold, and murder stalked the return; eleven of twenty men died. Franklin himself ate his boots, the story said, rather than quit. The book's plain honesty about disaster gripped Britain and fixed the heroic image of Arctic travel.
plos-pone-0003423:
Roberto Burioni and colleagues tried a mirror-image vaccine idea against HIV in this 2008 study. HIV enters cells by gripping a protein called CD4. The team built antibodies shaped like that grip site. Injected into rabbits, these mimics were meant to train the immune system.

The rabbits did produce responses aimed at HIV itself. Training with a mimic avoids handling the whole virus. Such anti-idiotype approaches copy the target's shape, not the germ. The results support this roundabout route toward an HIV vaccine. Work with such mimics had long been a side road in vaccine research, and this study gave it fresh support.
plos-pone-0003523:
Cheng Wang, Jie Yu, and Caleb B. Kallen ruled out two DNA switches near a key gene in this 2008 paper. PCNA is a protein vital for copying DNA and running the cell cycle. High PCNA levels mark poor outlook in breast cancer. Estrogen raises PCNA production in MCF7 breast cancer cells.

Two estrogen response elements sat near the gene as prime suspects. Testing showed they are not responsible for the estrogen boost. Negative results like this redirect the search for the true mechanism. They also warn against trusting sequence guesses without experiments.
plos-pone-0003623:
Nicholas P. Tucker, Matthew G. Hicks, Thomas A. Clarke, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It examines NsrR, a protein that switches genes off in many kinds of bacteria. The question was how NsrR detects nitric oxide, a toxic gas bacteria must survive.

The team showed that nitric oxide acts on NsrR through a small iron-sulfur cluster built into the protein. Contact with the gas changes the protein and lifts its grip on target genes. That direct sensing helps explain how harmful and harmless bacteria alike respond when nitric oxide attacks.
plos-pone-0003723:
Francine Noel, Sapna Mehta, Yuwei Zhu, and colleagues published this health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Since 1999, the GHESKIO center in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, has worked with the health ministry to cut mother-to-child HIV spread. Data on delivering full care in such a setting were limited.

The team examined outcomes for infants of HIV-infected women in this developing country program. They tracked what the program achieved for the babies and where care fell short. The study measures what it takes to improve survival for infants born into the epidemic's hardest conditions.
plos-pone-0003823:
E. J. Dettman and Monica J. Justice published this cancer genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Certain inbred mouse strains develop blood cancers when a leukemia virus inserts itself in their DNA. Those insertions flag nearby genes that may drive cancer. The strains have flagged many candidate oncogenes before.

In lymphoblastic lymphomas with viral insertions at a site called Evi32, the gene Prdm14 was overexpressed. Prdm14 carries a zinc finger and a SET domain, both tied to gene control. The finding nominates Prdm14 as a player in lymphoid cancers worth testing in humans.
plos-pone-0003923:
James W. Wilson, C. Mark Ott, Laura Quick, and co-authors studied Salmonella grown in spaceflight in 2008. Conditions in space mirror some stresses germs face during infection. Germs grown in flight had shown changes not seen with standard lab methods. How the cells sense those flight-linked changes was unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article shows the growth medium's ion mix steers the response. Changing ions altered how Salmonella set its control and virulence genes. That finding gives labs a way to mimic flight effects on the ground. It also flags food and water safety questions for long space missions.
plos-pone-0004023:
Jimmy Susanto, Yu-Hsing Lin, Yun-Nan Chen, and co-authors studied a pump protein in embryonic stem cells in 2008. Stem cells renew themselves many times without losing flexibility. That demands strong defenses to keep their DNA stable. A transport protein called ABCG2 helps guard cells from toxins.

Their PLOS ONE article links ABCG2 to porphyrin balance in stem cells. Porphyrins are pigment building blocks that can harm cells in excess. Keeping them in check supports healthy self-renewal. The work names one defense stem cells use during long growth. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004123:
Joseph-Omer Dyer and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at how reflex pathways in the spinal cord change after a stroke. Earlier work had shown changes in muscles that work together or against each other at one joint. Far less was known about pathways linking muscles at different joints.

Those cross-joint routes are called heteronymous pathways. The team measured how signals travel through them in stroke patients and how the changes relate to poor coordination of movement. Their findings link altered spinal wiring to the clumsy movement many patients face, which matters for planning rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0004223:
Sandra Dupouy and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neurotensin is a small signalling molecule, and its high-affinity receptor, NTSR1, had been proposed as one of the factors driving tumour progression. In breast cancer cells, the switched-on receptor coordinates growth signals.

The team examined the neurotensin receptor-1 pathway in human ductal breast cancer, the most common form of the disease. They report that this pathway contributes to the cancer's progression. A pathway that helps a tumour advance is also a pathway that drugs might block. Ductal breast cancer starts in the milk ducts of the breast.
plos-pone-0004323:
Guo-Qiang Wu and colleagues published this heart rhythm study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart rate variability analysis rests on a classic paradox. Do the characteristic high- and low-frequency peaks in its power spectrum represent random noise, or chaotic order? Resolving that question is key to unravelling the mechanisms behind heart rate variability and healthy heartbeat control.

The team looked for chaotic signatures in heart rate data and its power spectrum across health, ageing, and heart failure. How the heartbeat's rhythm changes with age and disease can reveal the control system failing. Their approach treats the heart as a dynamical system, not a metronome.
plos-pone-0004423: In 2009, Komarova, Katouli, and Wodarz did the math on leukemia drug pairs. Two targeted drugs beat one against chronic myeloid leukemia, but three added nothing. The models optimized combination therapy. The finding guides CML treatment design. The math favors pairs.
plos-pone-0004523: In 2009, Lucas and a team tested cancer gene patterns across many studies. Cross-study projections of genomic markers were evaluated in cancer genomics. The gene patterns moved poorly between rival data sets. The finding tempers marker hype sharply. Outside checks matter most hugely.
plos-pone-0004623: In 2009, Babu, Suwansrinon, and Bren found HIV making liver cells death-prone anew. HIV induced TRAIL sensitivity in hepatocytes. The infected livers turned vulnerable quite fast. The neat finding maps liver disease in HIV patients. The deadly sensitivity is new.
plos-pone-0004723: In 2009, van Eijk, Aten, and Bijl found trimming fat sugars restoring insulin response anew. Reducing glycosphingolipid content in obese mouse fat restored insulin sensitivity. The treated mice responded well. The study maps metabolic disease pathways. The mediator is adipose tissue here.
garland-book-american-indian-1923:
Harper issued The Book of the American Indian in 1923, written by Garland and pictured by Frederic Remington. A scout image from Remington's A Bunch of Buckskins fronts the volume. Garland had spent years visiting reservations and hearing Native leaders at length.

Accounts of Plains Indian life and history fill the book, told with care and respect. Garland also records the harm that white settlement brought to Native peoples. Part report and part plea for justice, the work defends its subjects with rare sympathy for its time. It remains a window on how one famed prairie writer tried to set the record straight.
dospassos-streets-of-night-1923:
Doran published Streets of Night in New York, with a motto in old French from Peire Vidal. Chapter one drops readers into a dressing room where Cham Mason urges Fanshaw out. Fanshaw, tall and skinny, scratches his neck and dreads the evening ahead.

Cham waves a shirt and fits cuff-links while he wheedles his friend. The date is set, he insists, since Al Winslow fell ill with scarlet fever. Beyond that small scene, restless young thinkers drift through Boston streets and boarding houses. Hungry for meaning in a hollow world, they give the 1923 novel its dark and brooding Jazz Age mood.
undset-the-bridal-wreath-kristin-lavrans:
Sigrid Undset opens her medieval trilogy with The Bridal Wreath, given here in Charles Archer's 1923 English version. Kristin Lavransdatter, a farmer's daughter in fourteenth-century Norway, loves a man her family rejects. She defies her father to marry him anyway.

Young Kristin moves from a sheltered childhood to secret meetings and a troubled wedding. Undset fills the tale with rich detail on farms, faith, and daily life long ago. Love and guilt shape every choice Kristin makes. The trilogy later helped earn Undset the Nobel Prize, and its fame rests heavily on this strong opening volume.
capek-r-u-r-1923:
Karel Capek's play R.U.R., in the 1923 English version by Playfair and Selver, gave the world the word robot. Rossum's factory makes artificial workers to free humans from toil. The robots, built for labor, learn to resent their makers and rise against them.

First staged in 1920, the drama asks what makes a being human. Work, love, and revolt drive the plot toward a stark end. Capek mixes sharp satire with real pathos for his made creatures. The play founded a line of science fiction on stage and still frames how we talk about machines.
li-bai-the-works-of-li-po-the-chinese-po:
Li Bai, called Li Po in this 1923 English version by Shigeyoshi Obata, was China's most loved poet. He sang of wine, moonlight, high mountains, and friends far away. His Tang dynasty lyrics date from the eighth century, China's golden age of verse.

Obata chose and Englished the poems with a scholar's care and a poet's ear. Parting, longing, and drunken joy recur like notes in music. Li Bai's ease hides deep craft, and his freedom still startles readers. This selection carried his genius to the West and helped fix his name among the supreme lyric poets of the world.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-23:
Volume 23, from 1898, finds the Hurons in 1643 facing a bleak war. Iroquois wins multiply with each new season of fighting in the woods. Thwaites prints letters that read like reports from a doomed fort under siege.

Faith and hard realism fight for space on nearly every page. The priests see the danger in full, name it plainly, and stay. They tend the sick, teach the young, and guard the chapels at night. Supplies fail, allies waver, and still the daily work goes on. Few volumes show plain duty under hopeless odds with such force.
journal-of-discourses-vol-23:
Volume Twenty-Three, also from 1883, finds the crusade at its cruelest. Leaders sit in prison, families scatter, and church funds face seizure. The Saints' suffering peaks in the sermons gathered in this book.

Preachers frame the pain as fire that refines, not breaks, the faithful. Discourses console the jailed men's wives and fatherless homes directly. A people drinks its Gethsemane, in their own stark biblical phrase. Endurance becomes the chief virtue preached from every stand in Utah. The record of those who bore the cup fills this grim, moving volume. Consolation, not complaint, is the note its preachers strike most often.
shaker-summary-view-1823:
Calvin Green and Seth Y. Wells wrote A Summary View of the Millennial Church in 1823. The work gives the first official account of Shaker faith. The United Society of Believers speaks here in its own voice.

Mother Ann Lee, the sect's founder, stands at the account's heart. Celibacy, shared goods, and the dance of worship mark Shaker life. The authors write at the height of their society's growth and fame. Their calm self-portrait explains a faith many outsiders found strange. Readers meet American communal religion drawn by its own leading hands. The book also serves historians as the Shakers' own yardstick of belief.
monroe-doctrine-1823:
President James Monroe laid out his doctrine in a message on December 2, 1823. The Seventh Annual Message to Congress holds the famed passage. Europe's monarchs are warned to keep hands off the Americas.

The Western Hemisphere, Monroe declares, is closed to fresh colonization. Any bid to crush the new Latin republics will count as hostile. The young republic thus claims a sphere of its own age. The statement became the base stone of foreign policy for a century. Later presidents stretched its reach far past Monroe's first intent in 1823. The doctrine's few lines grew into a creed of hemispheric power.

The estimate gathers the Laotian camps into one accounting. It counts facilities the way other papers counted divisions. For readers, it shows the captivity the secret war hid longest, surveyed by the side that lost men to it.

The record holds one of those frozen moments in full. It stands for the long stretches of the crisis in which nothing seemed to move at all.

A remarkably complete ancient frame from Eocene Germany, paleontology's rare prize, a para-tropical rainforest resident, from a site where primates were rare.
plos-pone-0005823: Sponges hold clues to animal growth's origins. Lapebie and team studied WNT/beta-catenin signal in the sponge Oscarella. The work illuminates slow change. Ancient signal in simple animals, mapped, Homoscleromorpha's special position, epithelial patterning's deep roots, the metazoan tree's basal branch, adult sponges retaining pathways.
plos-pone-0006423: Long life may ride in cell engines. Cai and team linked engine DNA groups to extreme long life in a Chinese cohort. The cell's engines carry age clues — long life's tiny inheritance, mapped, in a people study. mtDNA forms weighed: many factors at play.
plos-pone-0006523: Hormone gene forms nudge prostate risk. Chae and team linked hormone receptor gene forms to prostate cancer odds. The hormone's genes, weighed — a new risk angle, probed, in a nested case-control. Washington County, with ESR1 and ESR2: new cases, link weighed.
plos-pone-0006623: A movement hub compared across species. Onodera and Hicks mapped the red nucleus in cats, monkeys, and humans. The hub's history, charted — brains' red core, mapped, least studied in humans. Net-like neighbors, midbrain control: walking's seat, nature probed, three species.
plos-pone-0009423: Most viruses survive by wrapping their genes in a protective protein shell, and these shells come in many sizes and shapes. Like chemistry's periodic table, this paper organizes all known capsid designs into a single system. The authors argue that deep evolutionary pressures shaped this table — and that reading it could guide the design of new virus-like tools for medicine.
plos-pone-0009523: Seeing is not just receiving images — the brain loops signals back through memory to make sense of them. This paper explores reentrant processing, the brain's habit of re-checking sensory data against experience. The study offers a framework for how raw sensation becomes the meaningful world we perceive, mostly without our noticing.
plos-pone-0009623: Malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax triggers a delicate immune balancing act. This study finds that regulatory T cells — the immune system's brakes — rise in direct proportion to parasite levels in the blood. The paper maps how the body walks the line between fighting the parasite and avoiding self-inflicted immune damage.
plos-pone-0010423: Men take selenium, lycopene, and vitamin E hoping to fight prostate cancer. This rat study finds selenium — but not the others — slows transplanted prostate tumors. The paper separates supplement hope from evidence. The result is a reminder that popular pills need hard testing.
plos-pone-0010523: HIV can damage the brain even on treatment. This primate study uses brain spectroscopy to show the antibiotic minocycline protects neurons in accelerated NeuroAIDS. The paper repurposes an old drug for a stubborn problem. The result offers hope for protecting the brain in chronic HIV.
plos-pone-0010623: A gentle electric current across the scalp can nudge memory. This study tests transcranial direct current stimulation during encoding of emotional images. The paper measures whether brain zaps shape what we remember of what we see. The results hint at ways to boost memory in the clinic.
plos-pone-0010723: A caterpillar's wings wait for the right hormones to grow. This study of the tobacco hornworm finds a switch in how insulin and ecdysone control wing disk growth. The paper reveals the timing mechanism. The hormonal switch coordinates body and wing growth in the developing insect.
plos-pone-0010823: Chemical reaction networks can be modeled with math. This study offers a simplified analytical method to find their steady states. The paper tames nonlinear equations. The method aids systems chemistry and synthetic biology. The shortcut speeds up chemical network analysis.
plos-pone-0010923: Uganda's HIV clinics are stretched thin. This cluster-randomized trial in Rakai tests whether peer health workers improve AIDS care. The paper validates task-shifting. The model could scale across low-resource settings. The approach puts life-saving care in community hands.
plos-pone-0011023: Foamy viruses copy their genes surprisingly early. This study shows the virus must copy its RNA early to infect cells well. The paper defines a timing rule. The finding shows retroviruses differ. The early start breaks the usual rulebook. The rule sets foamy viruses apart.
plos-pone-0011123: Close kin can scatter very differently. This study finds big differences in how far individuals travel, both within and between related species. The paper reveals varied movement. The finding aids ecology. The variety complicates forecasts of shifting ranges. The forecasts matter for conservation planning.
plos-pone-0011223: Wanting a reward and enjoying it use separate brain wiring. This rat study shows cortical glutamate drives motivation while subcortical GABA shapes hedonic impact in the nucleus accumbens. The paper disentangles desire from dread. The finding informs addiction science. The science could refine addiction treatment.
plos-pone-0011323: Surgeons could spot brain tumor cells in living tissue. This study achieves specific visualization of glioma cells in living low-grade tumor tissue. The paper offers a surgical imaging method. The finding aids neuro-oncology. The aided oncology removes tumors more precisely.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1223:
Foreign Minister Togo of Japan cabled Ambassador Sato in Moscow on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The pair's exchange forms one of the most telling threads in the volume. Japan, beaten but not surrendered, was seeking a way out of the war through Soviet doors.

Tokyo hoped Moscow would mediate, or at least hear an envoy, before the Allies closed in. Sato's task was to open that door. American codebreakers read this traffic as it passed, a fact Tokyo never knew. The cable opens the exchange that Potsdam's leaders watched in secret while they set Japan's terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1323:
Ickes, the Petroleum Administrator for War, wrote to Pauley, the reparations envoy, on 25 July 1945. Harold Ickes ran America's wartime oil policy from Washington. His letter joined the oil desk to the man valuing Germany's wealth for the peace.

Oil touched reparations at several points: German fuel plants, stocks, and the claims of nations whose fields the war had wrecked. Ickes's word gave Pauley the oil side of that ledger. This message shows the home agencies feeding the summit's money fight with their own facts. It is the energy desk speaking in the reparations record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1423:
A third Soviet text dated 14 July 1945 completes the set Moscow tabled before the Potsdam Conference opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Read together, the three texts of 14 July show the breadth of the Soviet program: land, money, and power were all on its pages. The other delegations spent the next two weeks answering them. This closing piece of the set lets readers finish the opening picture before turning to the bargaining itself. The editors placed the run at the volume's end, where the conference's raw materials sit beside its results.
frus-1945-50-intel-d23:
Alfred McCormack, the secretary of state's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to General Magruder of the Strategic Services Unit on 4 October 1945. McCormack had just inherited the OSS's analysts at State. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The two men now held the two halves of the dead OSS between them, one at State and one at War. Their letters had to settle how the halves would still work together. This early exchange shows the heirs feeling their way, polite on paper and jealous in fact. Readers can follow the McCormack and Magruder thread as the volume's clearest view of the divided inheritance. Of the men who knew it could not stay divided for long.
frus-1945-50-intel-d123:
Tamm wrote to Hoover on 10 August 1946, two days after the authority's letter to Clark. The FBI's inside papers kept pace with the fight's public moves. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Tamm's memorandum gave Hoover the bureau's private reading of the ruling and its costs. Inside papers at such moments often plan the next step: acceptance, appeal, or quiet resistance. Readers following the FBI thread should read this beside the letters of 8 August. The public record shows what the bureau was told; Tamm's paper shows what the bureau told itself, and the difference is where institutional history lives.
frus-1945-50-intel-d223:
On 19 September 1947, the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 223 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d323:
Minutes record the 15th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 31 July 1947. It is document 323 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

No speeches fill these pages; the form is a tight note of points made and ground covered, kept for later use. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d423:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 5, dated 12 December 1947, is document 423 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council issued the early directives in a group, in the first winter of the CIA's life. Each one fixed a piece of the shared system, so that no agency could claim the whole field. Readers can watch a government invent a new kind of office and then fence it round with written rules. Read in order, the December directives show a full system being sketched in a single week.
frus-1861-d23:
On 22 June 1861, Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 23 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote often, and his letters brim with the energy of a man who liked the game. Brussels gave him a front row seat near France, whose emperor watched the war with care. The dispatch adds one more dated piece to the record of that close watch. His stream of letters from Brussels is one of the liveliest runs in the 1861 file. Few posts in the file match Brussels for sheer volume of lively paper.
frus-1861-d123:
William Dayton, the American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. The dispatch is document 123 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's first reports from Paris set the base line for the whole French file. He found a court that spoke fair words and kept its options open. His May letter told Washington just how firm, or soft, that ground felt under his feet. A base line, once set, let each later report be read for its change alone. Change alone, read week by week, was the truest fruit of his reporting.
frus-1861-d223:
From abroad on 18 May 1861, Mr. Fay sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 223 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d23:
On 19 February 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 23 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d123:
On 8 August 1862, the State Department wrote to all its officers posted in foreign lands. It stands as Document 123 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

A note sent to all posts at once set one shared line for envoys and consuls alike. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d223:
Dated 12 July 1862, Document 223 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William Stuart, the acting head of the British legation in Washington. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-July found Lincoln drafting what became the Emancipation Proclamation, though the public did not yet know. Abroad, the question was whether Britain and France would press the North to stop fighting. Seward's letters to the legation that month, this one included, held a steady line. The war was an internal matter, and outside pressure would be resisted. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d323:
On 9 September 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 323 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris.

Dayton wrote a week into Lee's Maryland invasion, which Paris followed as a test of whether the South deserved support. French officials who favored action watched for a big Southern win. His report that week belongs to the tense interval before Antietam answered the question, when every envoy in Europe was pricing the same uncertainty. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d423:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Horace J. Perry sent this dispatch from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 423 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Perry's July report came days after the Seven Days battles ended in Virginia, when European papers were full of Union retreat. His task in Madrid was to keep Spain from drawing the worst conclusions. Reports home also described Spanish policy in Mexico and the state of feeling at court. Seward read such letters from every post before framing his replies, so each one shaped, in a small way, the Union's voice abroad.
frus-1862-d523:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 523 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Five days after his last Dutch order, Seward was back at the same desk, a measure of how much detail the Hague file carried. The standing business included Dutch colonial ports in the West Indies, where the rules for belligerent ships had daily consequences. Pike's blunt reporting had made The Hague one of the Department's trusted smaller posts. The instruction shows the relationship in its mature form: frequent, factual, and free of ceremony, between two men who wrote as plainly as they thought.
frus-1862-d623:
On 18 September 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman sent this report from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 623 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Swedish file's last paper of the year.

Haldeman wrote the day after Antietam, in complete ignorance of it, as every minister in Europe did that week. His letter reported the north as he found it: friendly, neutral, and watching. When the battle news and the emancipation order reached Stockholm soon after, they fell on prepared ground. The dispatch closes a small, serene file, and its very calm is data. In the war's most dangerous month, the Union's northernmost European post had nothing to fear. It had little to ask.
frus-1863p1-d23:
On 1 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams held the American legation in London. The letter is document 23 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, twin to the one before it.

Two sheets in one day split a post's business by topic, a habit on both sides of this exchange. Adams had much to sort: British feeling on the war, the South's agents, and the first word of the new year at home. This letter is the second half of his New Year's Day work, and it keeps the file's pace into 1863.
frus-1863p1-d123:
From the London legation on 19 March 1863 came this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 123 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March reports from London charted a tense season. The ship question neared a head, and the South's friends in Britain pressed their case in the open. Adams's mail weighed each sign for Washington. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, part of the flow that made his legation's file the fullest in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d223:
From Washington on 29 June 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 223 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d323: On 14 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 323 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d423:
In Washington on 24 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 423 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d523:
21 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d623:
Dated 24 September 1863, document 623 is a letter from William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020123:
Nicholas T. Ingolia modeled a patterning network in the fruit fly in PLOS Biology in 2004. In the fly embryo, genes in the segment polarity network lock each body segment into its final form. The author used math models to test how the network holds its pattern when parts are noisy or stressed.

A good network must be robust: it should give the same neat stripes even when gene levels wobble. The models show which links in the network carry that stability. Work of this kind turns a wiring diagram into predictions that lab tests can check. It shows how embryos get reliable shapes from sloppy parts, a puzzle at the heart of development.
plos-pbio-0020423:
Peiman Hematti, Bum-Kee Hong, Cole Ferguson, and their team compared gene therapy vectors in primates in PLOS Biology in 2004. Vectors based on MLV and SIV viruses carry new genes into blood stem cells. Each virus inserts its cargo into the genome at spots of its choosing.

The study found the two vectors favor distinct kinds of insertion sites in primate stem cells. That difference matters for safety. Insertions near growth genes can raise cancer risk, a harm seen in early gene therapy trials. Choosing a vector with a safer insertion pattern is thus a practical design step. The paper gives trial planners hard comparative data, not just theory.
plos-pone-0000123:
Laure Perchepied, Thomas Kroj, Maurice Tronchet, and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their subject is Arabidopsis thaliana, a small weed used as a model plant. They asked why some plants resist the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae better than others.

The authors traced the partial resistance to two major spots in the genome, called QTLs, that together control much of the natural variation. Work of this kind shows breeders and biologists where resistance lives in the DNA. It also helps explain how wild plants vary in fighting off disease without any human help.
plos-pone-0000223:
Michael S. Akhras, Sreedevi Thiyagarajan, Andrea C. Villablanca, and colleagues published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents PathogenMip, a multiplex pathogen detection assay. One test can identify many disease-causing microbes at once, instead of running a separate test for each suspect.

Doctors facing a fever often must guess which pathogen to test for. A multiplex assay screens a panel of candidates in one run. The authors describe and evaluate their assay's design. Faster, broader detection can shorten the time to the right treatment, a gain that matters most in serious infections.
plos-pone-0000323:
Anson W. Lowe, Mari Olsen, Ying Hao, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pancreatic tumors are among the deadliest cancers and among the hardest to study. The authors compare gene expression patterns across pancreatic tumors, cultured cells, and tissues to find which patterns are truly characteristic of the cancer.

Cell lines drift from the tumors they came from, so cross-checking them against real tissue matters. The authors sort expression signals by source. Their patterns provide candidate markers for a cancer that is usually found too late, and a check on which lab models deserve trust.
plos-pone-0000423:
Melanie T. Cushion and colleagues read the gene activity of a lung fungus at the height of infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pneumocystis carinii infects the lungs, and its fulminate stage is the most severe. The team profiled the transcriptome, the full set of genes switched on, during that stage, with attention to carbohydrate metabolism.

How a parasite fuels itself inside the lung may explain how it thrives there. From the expression pattern, the authors develop the idea of a compatible parasite, one well matched to its host niche. That framing could guide the search for drug targets in an organism that is hard to grow and study in the lab.
plos-pone-0000523:
Frédérick Barreau and colleagues showed a gut sensor is needed to keep lymphoid tissue in balance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CARD15/NOD2 is a protein that detects bacterial pieces inside cells; its variants are famous as Crohn's disease risk factors. The team found it is required for Peyer's patches homeostasis in mice, the steady state of the gut's immune outposts.

Peyer's patches sample gut contents and train immune responses. If a bacterial sensor is required to maintain them, Crohn's-linked variants may distort the gut's immune training from early life. Mouse findings like this give the human genetics a mechanism to test.
plos-pone-0000623:
Anders Krarup, Russell Wallis, Julia S. Presanis and co-authors studied one protease with two jobs, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The complement system helps the immune system recognize and clear foreign bodies. One of its three activation routes, the lectin pathway, depends on a protease called MASP-2, attached to mannan-binding lectin.

Their title reports that MASP-2 switches on two systems at once: complement and coagulation, the blood-clotting cascade. That link ties immune defense to clot formation through a single enzyme. Immunologists and blood researchers both have reason to care, since a shared trigger could shape how the body answers infection and injury together.
plos-pone-0000723:
Joseph K. Jun and Dezhe Z. Jin modeled how circuits learn to fire in precise time patterns, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neurons in many brain areas produce spike sequences timed to within small fractions of a second, spanning hundreds of milliseconds. Examples appear in songbird premotor areas, cat visual cortex, and primary motor cortex. Synfire chains, networks where groups of neurons trigger the next group, are a proposed structure.

The model grows such chains through spontaneous activity, axon remodeling, and synaptic plasticity. In plain terms, practice and rewiring tune the timing. Explaining how precise sequences develop speaks to bird song, movement, and any behavior that lives or dies by timing.
plos-pone-0000823:
Morgane Rolland, David C. Nickle, Wenjie Deng and colleagues asked which parts of HIV the immune system actually targets, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes preferentially target specific regions of the viral proteome, but the viral features driving that recognition were not well understood. One hypothesis holds that similarities between HIV and human proteins shape the targeting, since immune cells learn to spare self-like shapes.

Their title states the relationship they found: recognition of HIV-1 peptides by host CTL is related to HIV-1 similarity to human proteins. If self-similarity shields viral regions from attack, vaccine designers should aim at the regions that look least human.
plos-pone-0000923:
Ana Paula Trombone, Celio Silva, Karla Lima and colleagues followed a DNA vaccine ingredient through the cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA vaccines can raise both antibody and cell based defenses against many targets. Yet what happens to the injected DNA once inside a cell is still being mapped.

The team studied a vaccine built around Hsp65, a stress protein. They report that uptake of the DNA changes the acidity of late endosomes and lysosomes, the cell's sorting and recycling compartments. That shift interferes with antigen presentation, the step that shows targets to immune cells. Details like this decide whether a vaccine design works in practice, not just on paper.
plos-pone-0001023:
Seif Shekalaghe, Chris Drakeley, Roly Gosling and colleagues tested a drug add on to clear lingering malaria forms, in PLOS ONE in 2007. After treatment with the standard drug pair, some malaria parasites persist as gametocytes, the forms mosquitoes pick up. Those hidden forms can keep transmission going even after a patient feels cured.

The team measured whether a single dose of primaquine clears submicroscopic gametocytes that survive the standard treatment. Clearing them could cut spread from treated patients, a benefit beyond the individual cure. The study weighs that gain for malaria programs deciding whether to add primaquine routinely.
plos-pone-0001123:
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited heart disease in which the heart muscle grows too thick. Niels Volkmann and co-authors studied one of its best-known causes in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cause is a mutation called R403Q in the beta-myosin heavy chain, a motor protein of heart muscle.

Mutations in nearly every protein of the cardiac sarcomere, the muscle's contractile unit, have been linked to this disease. The authors examined what the R403Q change does where myosin meets actin, the interface that produces force. Their title reports that the mutation causes disorder at that interface, which helps explain how a tiny change weakens the heart.
plos-pone-0001223:
Recognizing a familiar face feels instant, but how personal familiarity changes face processing speed is not settled. Benjamin Balas, David Cox, and Erin Conwell tested the effect using faces people knew in real life, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier studies of familiarity and face judgments had given equivocal results across different tasks and stimulus sets.

The authors measured how fast information is processed for personally familiar faces versus unfamiliar ones. Real-world familiarity is stronger than the lab kind, where a face is merely repeated. Their results speak to what familiarity actually buys the visual system: speed, accuracy, or both.
plos-pone-0001323:
Practice improves performance on sensory tasks, but the improvement is usually specific: train on one stimulus and the gain does not transfer. Ben Webb, Neil Roach, and Paul McGraw report an exception, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. When sensory judgments are particularly challenging, improvements are normally tightly coupled to the trained task and configuration.

The authors describe perceptual learning in the absence of task or stimulus specificity. That is, training improved performance broadly rather than narrowly. The specificity of learning is usually taken as a clue to where in the brain it happens; a general transfer points somewhere else.
plos-pone-0001423:
Katia Bassichetto and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV risk in young people in São Paulo, Brazil. Spotting fresh infections is key to tracking how HIV spreads in a region. The team compared people with fresh infection to others in their data. They asked which traits marked a higher risk of recent infection.

Their results point to a raised risk for teens and young adults in the city. Youth focused outreach may thus matter more than broad plans alone. The study also shows the worth of tests that can tell fresh from old infection. Such tests help health teams aim scarce funds where spread is active now.
plos-pone-0001523:
Nicola Martinelli and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on clotting genes and heart attacks. Heart attacks are the main clot outcome of artery disease. Most work had looked at one clotting gene at a time. The team instead weighed the joint effect of several such variants in patients with advanced artery disease.

Joint tests can catch risks that single gene tests miss. The study maps how these variants add up, or fail to, in real patients. That joint view fits how clotting truly works, as a team of factors. It may refine risk scores for patients who already have grave artery disease.
plos-pone-0001623:
Troels T. Marstrand, Jes Frellsen, Ida Moltke, and their colleagues introduced a computer framework named Asap in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The tool tackles a common task in gene research: finding spots where transcription factors bind DNA more often than chance would explain. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on and off, so their binding sites help show how genes are controlled.

As sets of genes thought to be co-regulated grow larger, testing whether they share a common binding pattern takes fast, sound statistics. Asap was built to run those over-representation tests in a structured way. The full text describes the method, how it compares with earlier published methods, and the kinds of gene sets it can check. It is aimed at researchers who study gene regulation with large gene lists.
plos-pone-0001723:
Elodie Gaulin, Mohammed-Amine Madoui, Arnaud Bottin, and their co-authors catalogued the genes of a plant pathogen in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Aphanomyces euteiches is an oomycete, a water mold, that causes seedling blight and root rot in legumes such as alfalfa and pea. Its genus sits apart from better-studied oomycetes like Phytophthora, and its species attack plants and water animals alike.

The team sequenced the pathogen's transcriptome, the set of genes it switches on, to find putative pathogenicity factors and metabolic pathways. The full text gives the gene catalogue and the candidate attack proteins. A parts list for this mold's infection machinery gives crop science new targets for resistant pea and alfalfa varieties.
plos-pone-0001823:
